story: Alaska's SNAP bill under Public Law 119-21. The federal share of SNAP administrative costs fell from 50 percent to 25 percent on October 1st, and the error-rate benefit cost share that follows will be set by an eligibility operation still running on a COBOL mainframe
stories_surviving: Alaska's SNAP bill under Public Law 119-21 (admin share cut, error-rate cost share, eligibility modernization)
Yukon fall chum, ADF&G Fall Update #9 (big run, small Canadian share)
DeepGreen Cook Inlet subsea data center, intervenors and the November 2nd FERC comment deadline

claims.claim: Public Law 119-21 sets the federal share of state SNAP administrative costs at 50 percent through fiscal year 2026 and 25 percent from fiscal year 2027 onward.
claims.verbatim: agency, through fiscal year 2026, 50 percent, and for fiscal year 2027 and each fiscal year thereafter, 25 percent,
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Congress, Public Law 119-21, sec. 10106
claims.notes: Verified against the showrunner's verbatim extraction out/2026-10-02/research/plaw119-21_sec10105-10106.txt (curl of the GPO text, line breaks normalized). Sec. 10106 amends 7 U.S.C. 2025(a). Enactment date July 4th, 2025 is from the public law's enactment record, not from the extracted lines. Background-dated primary source; the change took effect in the window.

claims.claim: Alaska's Legislative Finance Division says federal fiscal year 2027 begins October 1st, 2026, when SNAP administrative cost sharing changes to 25 percent federal and 75 percent state.
claims.verbatim: In federal fiscal year (FFY) 2027, which begins October 1, 2026, the cost sharing percentages will change to 25% federal and 75% state.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: Fact-checker fetched the PDF and read page 2 as an image; matches the showrunner's pypdf extraction. The paper is undated; its table uses YTD data through 9/30/25 and it says FFY25/26 error data is not yet available, so it was written between October 2025 and June 2026. date_of_source left blank rather than guessed. The paper also says the change applies to all states regardless of error rates.

claims.claim: NPR reported on October 1st that states must now cover 75 percent of SNAP operational costs while federal funding shrinks by half.
claims.verbatim: But starting on Thursday, states will need to cover 75% of that tab while federal funding shrinks by half.
claims.source_outlet: NPR (Juliana Kim), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: In window. Page credit reads NPR, By Juliana Kim, Published October 1, 2026. Thursday is October 1st. The preceding sentence says the federal government and states have historically split operational costs evenly. The article does not mention Alaska. Corroborates C01 and C02.

claims.claim: By the federal government's own calculations, the administrative cost change will cut federal SNAP spending by 16.9 billion dollars over five years, according to NPR.
claims.verbatim: By the federal government's own calculations, the new rule will lead to a $16.9 billion reduction in federal spending for SNAP over the next five years, or $3.4 billion annually.
claims.source_outlet: NPR (Juliana Kim), republished by Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: A national projection, not an Alaska figure. Hedge it as a federal estimate reported by NPR. Underlying federal calculation (likely CBO) not fetched. Internally consistent, 3.4 x 5 = 17.0, close to 16.9.

claims.claim: Under Public Law 119-21, a state with a SNAP payment error rate under 6 percent pays none of the benefit cost once the state cost share applies, starting in fiscal year 2028.
claims.verbatim: less than 6 percent, the Federal share of the cost of the allotment described in paragraph (1) for that State in a fiscal year shall be 100 percent, and the State share shall be 0 percent;
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Congress, Public Law 119-21, sec. 10105
claims.notes: Showrunner's verbatim extraction used. The clause opens 'Subject to clause (iii), beginning in fiscal year 2028', so the start year is subject to the delays in C10 and C11. NPR (October 1st) corroborates the 6 percent threshold and an October 2027 start, which is federal FY2028.

claims.claim: Under Public Law 119-21, a state with a payment error rate of at least 6 percent but under 8 percent pays 5 percent of SNAP benefit costs.
claims.verbatim: equal to or greater than 6 percent but less than 8 percent, the Federal share of the cost of the allotment described in paragraph (1) for that State in a fiscal year shall be 95 percent, and the State share shall be 5 percent;
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Congress, Public Law 119-21, sec. 10105
claims.notes: Showrunner's verbatim extraction used.

claims.claim: Under Public Law 119-21, a state with a payment error rate of at least 8 percent but under 10 percent pays 10 percent of SNAP benefit costs.
claims.verbatim: equal to or greater than 8 percent but less than 10 percent, the Federal share of the cost of the allotment described in paragraph (1) for that State in a fiscal year shall be 90 percent, and the State share shall be 10 percent;
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Congress, Public Law 119-21, sec. 10105
claims.notes: Showrunner's verbatim extraction used.

claims.claim: Under Public Law 119-21, a state with a payment error rate of 10 percent or more pays 15 percent of SNAP benefit costs.
claims.verbatim: equal to or greater than 10 percent, the Federal share of the cost of the allotment described in paragraph (1) for that State in a fiscal year shall be 85 percent, and the State share shall be 15 percent.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Congress, Public Law 119-21, sec. 10105
claims.notes: Showrunner's verbatim extraction used. The tiers top out at 15 percent; there is no higher tier.

claims.claim: From fiscal year 2029 on, the law sets each state's SNAP benefit cost share using its payment error rate from the third fiscal year before.
claims.verbatim: the Secretary shall use the payment error rate of the State for the third fiscal year preceding the fiscal year for which the State share is being calculated.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Congress, Public Law 119-21, sec. 10105
claims.notes: Showrunner's verbatim extraction used. Derived reading, which the deck must present as arithmetic on the statute and not as an agency statement: the third fiscal year before FY2029 is FY2026, the federal year that ended September 30th. For FY2028 only, a state may elect its FY2025 or FY2026 rate (clause (ii)(I)).

claims.claim: The law delays the benefit cost share to fiscal year 2029 for any state whose fiscal year 2025 payment error rate, multiplied by 1.5, is 20 percent or more.
claims.verbatim: If, for fiscal year 2025, the payment error rate of a State multiplied by 1.5 is equal to or above 20 percent, the implementation date under clause (i) for that State shall be fiscal year 2029.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Congress, Public Law 119-21, sec. 10105
claims.notes: Showrunner's verbatim extraction used. Arithmetic, 20 / 1.5 = 13.33 recurring, so any rate of 13.333...% or higher qualifies. AP (C15) rounds this to 13.34%. Alaska's FY2025 rate of about 23% (C13, C14) times 1.5 is about 34.5%, well over 20.

claims.claim: The law moves the start to fiscal year 2030 for any state whose fiscal year 2026 payment error rate, multiplied by 1.5, is also 20 percent or more.
claims.verbatim: If, for fiscal year 2026, the payment error rate of a State multiplied by 1.5 is equal to or above 20 percent, the implementation date under clause (i) for that State shall be fiscal year 2030.
claims.source_outlet: U.S. Congress, Public Law 119-21, sec. 10105
claims.notes: Showrunner's verbatim extraction used. Same threshold, 20 / 1.5 = 13.33 recurring. The statute text does not say 'also'. Read literally, clause (II) turns on the FY2026 rate alone. For Alaska, already in the FY2029 group, the effect is the same. Alaska's FY2026 rate is not published (USDA normally releases it around June 2027), so no source yet says whether Alaska will reach FY2030. Do not imply either outcome.

claims.claim: Alaska erred in 23 percent of SNAP payments made in 2025, the Anchorage Daily News reported.
claims.verbatim: Alaska erred in 23% of payments made in 2025
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: Background (June). Independently corroborated by AP (C13, 'over 23%'). This is federal FY2025, released by USDA in June 2026. The primary USDA FNS payment error rate page (fns.usda.gov/snap/qc/per) returned HTTP 403 to the fact-checker, so no primary document was reached for this figure. Two independent outlets agree.

claims.claim: The Associated Press reported that Alaska had the highest SNAP payment error rate in the nation, at over 23 percent, and would benefit from the delay.
claims.verbatim: The delay will benefit Alaska, which had the highest error rate of over 23%.
claims.source_outlet: Associated Press (David A. Lieb), via Alaska's News Source
claims.notes: Background (June). The page timestamp reads Jun. 24, 2026 at 6:04 PM AKDT, although the URL path says 06/25. The same AP passage names Delaware, Georgia, Illinois, New Mexico, Oregon and the District of Columbia as the other jurisdictions receiving the delay.

claims.claim: AP reported that states with error rates of at least 13.34 percent last year get a delay in their cost share until at least fiscal year 2029.
claims.verbatim: States with error rates of at least 13.34% last year will receive a delay in their cost-share requirements until at least the 2029 fiscal year.
claims.source_outlet: Associated Press (David A. Lieb), via Alaska's News Source
claims.notes: AP's 13.34% is the statute's 20 / 1.5 = 13.33 recurring rounded up. A slide should either cite the statute's 1.5 and 20 percent (C10) or say 'about 13.3 percent'. Presenting 13.34 as an exact statutory number would be wrong. 'At least the 2029 fiscal year' reflects the possible further delay in C11.

claims.claim: Alaska had the highest SNAP payment error rate in the nation for the fourth consecutive year, the Anchorage Daily News reported.
claims.verbatim: Alaska's federal food assistance program had the highest error rate in the nation for the fourth consecutive year, according to data recently published by federal officials.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: Background. The 'highest in the nation' ranking for 2025 is corroborated by AP (C13). The four-year streak rests on ADN alone, so attribute it to ADN.

claims.claim: Alaska's SNAP payment error rate was 57 percent in federal fiscal year 2022, according to the Legislative Finance Division.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: Table row on page 1. The fact-checker read the rendered PDF image to confirm the columns: State Fiscal Year, Final Budget, Active ET PCNs, Average Filled, Average Vacancy, SNAP Error Rate By FFY, Penalties. Each row's error rate is labeled by FFY. ADN independently gives 57% in 2022.

claims.claim: Alaska's SNAP payment error rate was 60.4 percent in federal fiscal year 2023, according to the Legislative Finance Division.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: Confirmed in the rendered table. ADN rounds it to 60% ('57% in 2022, 60% in 2023 and 25% in 2024'). The paper says the FFY23 rate was largely driven by a misunderstanding of federal policy on required recertification intervals.

claims.claim: Alaska's SNAP payment error rate was 24.7 percent in federal fiscal year 2024, according to the Legislative Finance Division.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: Confirmed in the rendered table. ADN rounds to 25%. The paper says the FFY24 rate was largely due to a decision to keep issuing benefits to Alaskans still in recertification because of the persistent backlog.

claims.claim: Alaska's SNAP error rate averaged 15.3 percent between federal fiscal years 2014 and 2024, according to the Legislative Finance Division.
claims.verbatim: Alaska's SNAP error rate between FFYs 2014 and 2024 averaged 15.3%.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: Page 2. Apostrophe straightened in the verbatim field. The original reads Alaska’s. The paper notes the average includes the high FFY2023 and FFY2024 rates.

claims.claim: The average vacancy rate among Alaska's eligibility technician positions in Public Assistance Field Services was 34.3 percent in state fiscal year 2025.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: Confirmed in the rendered table (column 'Average Vacancy of Eligibility Tech PCNs'). Cross-check, 1 - 218/332 = 34.3%, consistent. The SFY2026 row (FY26 enacted, YTD to 9/30/25) shows 16.4%. That row is partial-year, so don't present it as a full-year result.

claims.claim: Alaska had 332 active eligibility technician positions in state fiscal year 2025 and an average of 218 of them filled.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: Same row as C20, confirmed in the rendered image. The positions are in the Public Assistance Field Services allocation.

claims.claim: The total cost of administering SNAP in Alaska averaged 26.5 million dollars a year over the last five years, according to the Legislative Finance Division.
claims.verbatim: Over the last five years, the total cost of administering SNAP in Alaska has averaged $26.5 million per year
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: Page 2, confirmed in the rendered image.

claims.claim: The Legislative Finance Division estimates Alaska's annual share of SNAP administrative costs will rise by about 6.6 million dollars in state fiscal year 2027.
claims.verbatim: meaning Alaska's annual share of administrative costs will increase by approximately $6.6 million in state fiscal year (FY) 2027.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: An estimate. Write 'about' or 'estimated'. Apostrophe straightened in the verbatim field. Arithmetic, 25 points of $26.5M = $6.625M, consistent. This figure DIFFERS from ADN's 'nearly $11 million annually' (C24). Keep each attributed to its own source and don't reconcile them. Neither source explains the other's figure. A possible but unverified reason is a different cost base or a different year span. SFY2027 began July 1st, 2026, so the federal change hits only three quarters of it, which might make the SFY figure smaller than a full-year one. This is unverified. Do not state it.

claims.claim: The Anchorage Daily News reported that the administrative cost shift is set to increase Alaska's SNAP expenses by nearly 11 million dollars a year.
claims.verbatim: a change that is set to increase Alaska's expenses on SNAP by nearly $11 million annually.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: Disputed magnitude. It conflicts with the Legislative Finance Division's $6.6 million (C23). If both are used, show them side by side and attribute each, for example 'nearly $11 million a year, according to the Anchorage Daily News'. ADN does not name the source of its figure.

claims.claim: SNAP serves more than 66,000 Alaskans, roughly 9 percent of the state's population, the Anchorage Daily News reported.
claims.verbatim: The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, formerly known as food stamps, serves more than 66,000 Alaskans, or roughly 9% of the state's population.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: Background. The same article also says 'As of last year, average participation dropped below 65,000', so prefer 'more than 65,000' or attribute the 66,000 to ADN. Single-sourced. Sanity check, 66,000 / about 740,000 residents = 8.9%, consistent with 9%.

claims.claim: Alaska was fined nearly 12 million dollars in 2024 for its high SNAP error rates.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: LegFin's table lists Penalties/Fines (approx., in thousands) of $11,908.7 for SFY2024, with the footnote '2024 Penalty: For activity between 2022-2023. Half of the penalty will be reinvested in infrastructure.' Corroborated by ADN: 'nearly $12 million in 2024 and $4.6 million in 2025'. If the deck says the fine covered 2022 to 2023 errors, cite the footnote.

claims.claim: Alaska was fined 4.6 million dollars in 2025 for its SNAP error rate in 2024.
claims.verbatim: 2025 Penalty: For activity in 2024.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Legislative Finance Division, Informational Paper 25-1
claims.notes: The amount is in the SFY2025 row as $4,600.0 thousand, and the footnote gives the activity year. ADN independently says $4.6 million in 2025.

claims.claim: The Anchorage Daily News reported, citing Alaska Department of Health data, that Alaska could owe more than 42 million dollars a year for SNAP benefits if its error rate is not below 10 percent when the cost share begins.
claims.verbatim: it could be liable to pay more than $42 million for its SNAP benefits to the federal government beginning that year, according to data presented by the Alaska Department of Health earlier this year.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: Projection, so it needs a hedge like 'could', 'according to state Health Department data reported by ADN'. 'That year' refers back to the delay 'until 2029'. ADN's phrase 'lower its error rate below 10% by then' simplifies the statute. Under C09 the FY2029 share rests on the FY2026 rate, which is already fixed, so don't repeat the 'by then' framing. Implied annual benefit base is 42 / 0.15 = about $280M.

claims.claim: The Anchorage Daily News reported that Alaska would owe 28 million dollars if its error rate is between 8 and 10 percent.
claims.verbatim: The state would be liable for $28 million if the error rate is between 8% and 10%
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: Projection based on Health Department data as reported by ADN. Consistent with C28 (28 / 0.10 = $280M base).

claims.claim: The Anchorage Daily News reported that Alaska would owe nearly 17 million dollars if its error rate is between 6 and 8 percent.
claims.verbatim: and nearly $17 million if the error rate is between 6% and 8%.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: INTERNAL INCONSISTENCY. The 15% and 10% tiers both imply a base of about $280M, but 17 / 0.05 = $340M, and 5% of $280M would be about $14M. Either the Department's slide used different assumptions or the figure was transcribed wrong. The primary Department of Health presentation was not found. Recommend not charting the three tiers as one proportional staircase. If used, attribute it and keep it off a scaled visual.

claims.claim: Alaska's Department of Health says its legacy eligibility system, EIS, is built in COBOL on a mainframe and is difficult to change.
claims.verbatim: it is built in an old technology (COBOL on a mainframe) that is difficult to change.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Health, EIS Modernization project repository (GitHub)
claims.notes: Showrunner's extraction used. The fact-checker also fetched the live repo page and confirmed this exact phrase appears. The README is undated and its 'Challenge' section dates from earlier phases (it says work on the previous plan ended summer 2016). Present it as the Department's own description in its repo, not as a fresh statement. The same section says EIS is expensive to host and its expertise is aging out.

claims.claim: Alaska's Department of Health says a prior contractor migration left it with a partially implemented eligibility system, ARIES, that contains only MAGI Medicaid.
claims.verbatim: leaving the State with a partially implemented eligibility system, ARIES, which at this time only contains MAGI Medicaid.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Health, EIS Modernization project repository (GitHub)
claims.notes: Exact phrase confirmed on the live page. 'At this time' is undated in the README, so hedge it as 'the Department's project repo says'. The 2026 Milestone 2.5 RFP (C35) still describes ARIES as supporting MAGI Medicaid and EIS as the legacy mainframe, which supports it being current.

claims.claim: The Department of Health says the state determines eligibility in two systems, which forces a good deal of manual workarounds.
claims.verbatim: The State is now determining eligibility in two systems forcing a good deal of manual workarounds so that the State can continue to deliver services.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Health, EIS Modernization project repository (GitHub)
claims.notes: Showrunner's extraction used. Undated README language, so attribute it to the repo. The README adds that working in two systems 'has caused a significant decrease in worker productivity'.

claims.claim: Alaska's Department of Health estimated a budget of 20 million dollars for Milestone 2 of its eligibility modernization, a time and materials contract.
claims.verbatim: We estimate a budget of $20,000,000.00 dollars for the completion of this project as outlined in the RFP. Proposals priced at more than this amount will be considered non-responsive.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Health, RFP-IES-Milestone2 repository (GitHub)
claims.notes: Showrunner's extraction used (escaped dollar sign removed). The figure is the RFP's budget estimate and proposal ceiling, NOT an awarded contract value. Write 'budgeted at up to $20 million'. The date is the RFP issue date on the page (March 24, 2025). Milestone 2 covers non-MAGI Medicaid categories and hospital presumptive eligibility (per the Milestone 2.5 README). The term is 18 months from award with one optional one-year renewal.

claims.claim: The Department of Health says its Milestone 2 procurement is complete and the project began in October 2025.
claims.verbatim: This procurement/acquisition is complete; the project began in October 2025.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Health, RFP-IEP-Milestone2.5 repository (GitHub)
claims.notes: Showrunner's extraction used. This supersedes the Milestone 2 RFP's planned 'Contract begins August 15, 2025'. Use October 2025 as the actual start. The vendor is not named in the README. Nava announced a 2.5-year DPA contract on September 29th, 2025 (C38), but no fetched page ties Nava to Milestone 2 specifically, so don't link them.

claims.claim: The Department of Health estimated a budget of 5 million dollars for Milestone 2.5, a time and materials contract planned to run about 18 months.
claims.verbatim: We estimate a budget of $5,000,000.00 dollars for the completion of this project as outlined in the RFP. Proposals priced at more than this amount will be considered non-responsive.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Health, RFP-IEP-Milestone2.5 repository (GitHub)
claims.notes: Budget estimate and ceiling, not an award. The README schedule says 'Contract begins July 2026' as a best estimate. No fetched page confirms the award or the start, so write 'planned' or 'scheduled'. The term reads 'This contract term is planned to be approximately 18 months.' The date is the RFP issue date on the page (January 22, 2026).

claims.claim: Milestone 2.5 is meant to migrate SNAP and non-MAGI Medicaid beneficiary data and reports from the mainframe into a modern data repository that is accessible by API.
claims.verbatim: Specifically, this project will migrate and convert beneficiary data, and related operational and administrative reports for the non-MAGI Medicaid programs and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP).
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Health, RFP-IEP-Milestone2.5 repository (GitHub)
claims.notes: The preceding sentence reads 'The objective of Milestone 2.5 is to migrate and convert the mainframe data and reports that are associated with Milestones 2 and 3, into a modern data repository that is accessible via API to all consumers.' The README describes EIS as 'A legacy mainframe system supporting eligibility determination and benefit administration for multiple public assistance programs.' No AI is mentioned.

claims.claim: Nava announced it won a two-and-a-half-year contract with the Division of Public Assistance in Alaska's Department of Health to support eligibility system modernization.
claims.verbatim: Nava is excited to announce we won a two-and-a-half-year contract with the Alaska Department of Health (DOH) Division of Public Assistance (DPA).
claims.source_outlet: Nava PBC
claims.notes: Company's own announcement, so it is primary for the fact that Nava won the contract. No dollar value is given. Scope: 'support DPA's ongoing modernization of the state's eligibility information system and integrated eligibility services.' Background-dated.

claims.claim: Nava co-founder and chief operating officer Sha Hwang said nearly one-third of Alaskans rely on Medicaid.
claims.verbatim: This work has crucial impacts since nearly one-third of Alaskans rely on Medicaid,
claims.source_outlet: Nava PBC
claims.notes: Verbatim quote by a named person, confirmed on two fetches. It is a vendor's characterization. Attribute it to Hwang and don't present it as a state statistic. Medicaid enrollment data was not fetched to corroborate it.

claims.claim: Department of Health spokesperson Mirna Estrada wrote that the most significant error rate improvements will not show until modernization is fully implemented, work scheduled for completion in 2028.
claims.verbatim: While we expect the error rate to continue declining year after year, the most significant improvements will not be reflected until these modernization efforts are fully implemented. That work is scheduled for completion in 2028,
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: Verbatim written statement from a named official, quoted by ADN. The 2028 completion is an agency schedule, so hedge it ('scheduled for', 'the department says'). Arithmetic for context: FY2029's share rests on FY2026 (C09) and FY2030's on FY2027, so a 2028 completion would first reach the rate for FY2028 and the cost share for FY2031. That is the fact-checker's derivation, not a source statement. Don't print it as fact without marking it as arithmetic.

claims.claim: Estrada wrote that workload backlogs had a larger impact on Alaska's error rate during the periods when they were significant.
claims.verbatim: During periods when Alaska had significant workload backlogs, that had a larger impact on the state's error rate,
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: Confirmed on two separate fetches. ADN paraphrases Estrada as saying federal quality control rules count benefits as erroneous when applications are not processed within 30 days (one week for expedited). That passage is a paraphrase, not a quote. Consistent with the Legislative Finance Division's FFY24 explanation (C18 notes).

claims.claim: The Anchorage Daily News reported that Senators Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski negotiated the reprieve delaying the cost share until 2029 for states with the highest error rates.
claims.verbatim: Alaska's Republican U.S. Sens. Dan Sullivan and Lisa Murkowski negotiated a reprieve that grants states with the highest SNAP error rates a delay in implementing those costs until 2029.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Iris Samuels)
claims.notes: A political attribution from one source. Attribute it to ADN. The statute (C10, C11) confirms the delay mechanism and the possible move to FY2030, but not who negotiated it.

claims.claim: ADF&G released Yukon River Fall Update #9, Fall Fishery Announcement #25, on September 22nd.
claims.verbatim: Released: September 22, 2026
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries
claims.notes: Fact-checker fetched the PDF and read pages 1 to 3 as images. Title: '2026 Yukon River Salmon Fall Fishery Announcement #25, Fall Update #9, Yukon Area Salmon Fishery'. In window.

claims.claim: ADF&G says the Yukon fall chum run is projecting to be greater than 900,000 fish, well above the upper end of the drainagewide escapement goal range.
claims.verbatim: Overall, the fall chum salmon run is projecting to be greater than 900,000 fish, well above the upper end of the drainagewide escapement goal range of 300,000
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries
claims.notes: Projection, so write 'projecting'. The verbatim stops at the range's dash. The page goes on with an en dash to '600,000 fish', so the range is 300,000 to 600,000.

claims.claim: ADF&G says the Canadian-origin share of Yukon fall chum is 15 percent, well below the historical average of 30 percent.
claims.verbatim: the proportion of Canadian-origin fall chum salmon (15%) is well below the historical average of 30%.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries
claims.notes: Page 1. The release says border goals 'may be met' but there is not enough certainty to support directed fishing on Canadian stocks.

claims.claim: Genetic mixed stock analysis applied to Pilot Station sonar estimates indicates about 914,000 fall chum were in the Yukon through September 7th, above the median of 822,000 for that date.
claims.verbatim: Genetic mixed stock analysis, when applied to the passage estimates indicate approximately 914,000 fall chum salmon are in the river, through September 7 (Figure 1). This is above the median cumulative passage of 822,000
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries
claims.notes: Page 2. The verbatim slightly exceeds 40 words, so trim it if needed. The same paragraph says the genetic fall chum timing was 9 days late at Pilot Station and all-chum fall-season passage was about 1,029,000.

claims.claim: Eagle sonar counted a cumulative 19,000 fall chum as of September 21st, below the median of 49,000 for that date.
claims.verbatim: As of September 21, the cumulative passage was 19,000 fall chum salmon which is below the median of 49,000 fish for this date
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries
claims.notes: Page 3, Eagle Sonar (ADF&G and DFO). The midpoint by median timing is September 23, so the count was taken before the run's typical midpoint. Hedge any 'missing fish' framing.

claims.claim: Teedriinjik (Chandalar) River sonar counted 168,300 fall chum as of September 21st, above the median of 139,600.
claims.verbatim: As of September 21, the cumulative passage was 168,300 fall chum salmon, which is above the median passage of 139,600 fish for this date.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries
claims.notes: Page 3, operated by USFWS. Sheenjek sonar on the same page reads 18,300 against a median of 31,700.

claims.claim: ADF&G projects the 2026 Yukon coho run at 116,000 fish, well below the historical average run index of 212,000.
claims.verbatim: the run projection based on historic late run timing is 116,000 fish, well below the historical average run index of 212,000 coho salmon.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries
claims.notes: Projection. The release adds that coho increased to a level able to support subsistence harvest.

claims.claim: The treaty objective for fall chum on the mainstem Yukon River is 70,000 to 104,000 fish.
claims.verbatim: The treaty objective (interim management escapement goal) for the mainstem Yukon River is 70,000
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries
claims.notes: The verbatim stops at the en dash. The page reads 70,000 to 104,000 fall chum for the mainstem and 22,000 to 49,000 for the Fishing Branch River, both written with en dashes, which are banned in house copy, so write 'to'.

claims.claim: ADF&G says the mainstem of the Porcupine River will stay closed until the Fishing Branch River escapement goal is projected to be met.
claims.verbatim: The mainstem of the Porcupine River will remain closed until the escapement goal on the Fishing Branch River is projected to be met.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Division of Commercial Fisheries
claims.notes: Page 1. The same paragraph says subsistence restrictions are being removed in most areas based on fall chum travel time.

claims.claim: The Center for Biological Diversity, the Alaska Commercial Fisheries Conservation Alliance and the Kenai Peninsula Borough have filed motions to intervene against DeepGreen's Cook Inlet application, ADN reported.
claims.verbatim: So far, motions to intervene have been filed by the Center for Biological Diversity, Alaska Commercial Fisheries Conservation Alliance and the Kenai Peninsula Borough.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Bella Biondini)
claims.notes: SINGLE-SOURCED. The FERC eLibrary docket was not fetched (no docket number in hand, and eLibrary is JavaScript-rendered). Attribute it to ADN and write 'so far', because more intervenors may have filed since September 24th.

claims.claim: DeepGreen Cook Inlet released plans for a 100-megawatt subsea data center with as many as 350 underwater turbines, ADN reported.
claims.verbatim: released plans for a 100-megawatt subsea data center with as many as 350 underwater turbines
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Bella Biondini)
claims.notes: Proposed, not approved. Write 'proposed' or 'plans'. The same sentence says 66 hives would house AI servers, with power and cooling from Cook Inlet water. The hives wording sits in quote marks on the page and was left out of the verbatim to avoid curly quotes. The preliminary permit is a study permit and does not authorize construction. Single-sourced to ADN, and the filing itself was not fetched.

claims.claim: FERC accepted DeepGreen's preliminary permit application for Cook Inlet on September 1st, opening a two-month public comment period, ADN reported.
claims.verbatim: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission accepted DeepGreen's preliminary Cook Inlet permit application on Sept. 1, triggering a two-month public comment period.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Bella Biondini)
claims.notes: Single-sourced to ADN, and the FERC notice was not fetched. Attribute it.

claims.claim: Comments, motions to intervene and competing applications can be filed online with FERC through November 2nd, ADN reported.
claims.verbatim: Residents can file comments, motions to intervene and competing applications online at ferconline.ferc.gov/QuickComment.aspx through Nov. 2.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Bella Biondini)
claims.notes: A call-to-action date. Consistent with D03, since September 1st plus two months is about November 1st, and November 1st, 2026 is a Sunday, so the deadline rolls to Monday, November 2nd. Single-sourced. Confirm on FERC's notice before printing it as a hard deadline.

claims.claim: The Alaska Commercial Fisheries Conservation Alliance's motion says DeepGreen did not assess effects on the more than 1,300 active commercial fishing permits in Upper Cook Inlet, ADN reported.
claims.verbatim: DeepGreen's proposal did not assess how a possible data center could affect the more than 1,300 active commercial fishing permits in the Upper Cook Inlet.
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Bella Biondini)
claims.notes: An intervenor's claim relayed by ADN, so attribute it to the motion. The motion also says the commercial salmon fishery historically brings 'nearly $10 million in revenue to the region'. That is one side's figure. The permit count was not checked against CFEC.

claims.claim: Cooper Freeman, Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, said the project does not belong in the inlet.
claims.verbatim: The scope and the scale and sort of insanity of this project just doesn't belong in the inlet,
claims.source_outlet: Anchorage Daily News (Bella Biondini)
claims.notes: CORRECTED WORDING. The scout's version read 'just belongs in the inlet', which reverses the meaning. The fetched page reads 'just doesn't belong in the inlet'. Use only this wording. It is one side's framing, so pair it with DeepGreen's position if the deck uses it. The fetched article did not quote DeepGreen.

killed.claim: Katie Bergh (CBPP) said states may have to 'find new sources of revenue, cut funding from other programs or further restrict access to SNAP'
killed.why: Not found verbatim on the NPR/Alaska Public Media page. The verified Bergh quotes are 'And we may see some states decide that they need to withdraw from the program entirely' and a line about eligible families in poorer states. If the deck needs Bergh, use one of those as a new claim, with the speaker attributed to CBPP.

killed.claim: Alaska is spending up to $25 million to replace its COBOL mainframe
killed.why: Adds two RFP budget estimates ($20M and $5M), which are proposal ceilings, not awarded contract values. Milestone 2.5 targets data migration, not full replacement, and its award is unconfirmed. Use C34 and C36 separately, as estimates.
August 15th was the RFP's planned contract start. The Department's later Milestone 2.5 README says the project began in October 2025 (C35). Superseded.

killed.claim: Nava's Form-Filling Assistant AI pilot is being used in Alaska
killed.why: The Nava page mentions a Form-Filling Assistant event, but nothing ties the tool to the Alaska contract. No fetched page supports Alaska use. Any AI angle on this story is unsourced.

killed.claim: Alaska's FY2026 SNAP payment error rate, or whether Alaska will be pushed to FY2030
killed.why: Not published. USDA normally releases FY rates the following June. No source states it, and the deck must not imply either outcome.

killed.claim: Alaska's FY2025 error rate from USDA FNS, as a primary source
killed.why: fns.usda.gov returned HTTP 403. The 23% figure survives on two independent secondary sources (ADN C12, AP C13), but no primary document was reached for it.

killed.claim: Alaska must cut its error rate below 10% by 2029 to avoid the top tier
killed.why: Misreads the statute. From FY2029 the share uses the third preceding fiscal year's rate (C09), so FY2029 rests on FY2026, which is already over. ADN's 'by then' wording is not reused.

killed.claim: The three liability tiers ($42M, $28M, nearly $17M) scale proportionally to one benefit base
killed.why: They don't. 42/0.15 and 28/0.10 both give about $280M, but 17/0.05 gives $340M. The underlying Health Department presentation was not found. The tiers are kept as attributed claims (C28 to C30) and are not drawn as one proportional chart.

killed.claim: Average SNAP participation dropped below 65,000 last year
killed.why: Appears on the ADN page but was only captured once. It was dropped to keep the claim set tight and is noted under C25 as a reason to hedge the 66,000 figure. The showrunner can promote it after a dedicated re-check.

killed.claim: 147 Chinook salmon were radio-tagged near Rampart Rapids in 2026
killed.why: On a PDF page beyond the three the fact-checker rendered (pages 1 to 3 of 9). Not verified this pass.

killed.claim: Upper Cook Inlet commercial salmon fishery brings nearly $10 million in revenue
killed.why: Not killed outright, but folded into the notes on D05 as an intervenor's figure. It is not a standalone claim because it was never checked independently.
